title: Rwanda (1994)
hook: in a country full of churches, genocide happened even inside them; the work of reconciliation goes on

segments.voice: Yesterday: peacemakers, hands too full for stones. Your line: candles and prayers. This week brought a nun, an archbishop, a union, a commission, grandmothers and candles. It ends with a harder story.

A brick church in a Rwandan village. Inside, on the long benches, there are no people. There are clothes. Piles of them, faded shirts and dresses and small sweaters, left where they were found. The church is a memorial now. People ran to it because a church was supposed to be safe. It wasn't. This lesson is heavy, and it's fine to pause it and come back. Today: what happened in the churches, and what Christians there are still doing about it.
screen: `A CHURCH WAS SUPPOSED TO BE SAFE.`

segments.voice: Rwanda is a small, green, hilly country in east-central Africa, and church was part of ordinary life there: Catholic, Anglican, Adventist, Pentecostal. Then came the genocide against the Tutsi. Neighbors killed neighbors, urged on by radio, with machetes and guns. Hutu who refused or who hid people were killed too. Tutsi families fled to churches, as they had in earlier troubles, and in some of those churches they were massacred. The honest part has to be said plainly. Some clergy and church workers took part, or handed people over, or stayed silent, and some were later tried and convicted. Some historians trace how colonial rulers and missionaries had hardened the line between Hutu and Tutsi long before. And some priests, nuns, pastors and ordinary believers hid people in their homes and ceilings, and some died for it. Both are true. The Bible has words for both. When Cain kills his brother, God says in the King James Bible: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground." And the first letter of John: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar." Afterward, Rwandan church leaders asked forgiveness, and so did the pope. Churches left some buildings as memorials rather than painting over them. Church groups now run reconciliation work: survivors and people who killed, meeting in small groups, sometimes for a long time, telling the truth and slowly learning to live on the same hill. Never again is easy to say. These are people trying to mean it.

Picture terraced hillsides in morning mist, a woman carrying water up a path, a minibus climbing a red-earth road; all of that is Rwanda too. Then, without trying to imagine the violence, hold the survivors, still living with what they saw, and those making peace with neighbors who wronged them. If you pray, pray for Rwanda, for survivors, and for those doing the slow work of reconciliation.
Rwanda. A country of churches where genocide reached inside them, where some believers betrayed and others rescued, and where reconciliation work continues.
Your line: never again, truly. People on the same hill, trying to mean it. Take care until tomorrow.

chat.says: How could churches in Rwanda be part of a genocide? Weren't churches safe places?
options: Some clergy betrayed people while other believers hid them and died; both are true, and churches now work at healing.
Churches stayed neutral: no clergy took any part, and everyone who reached one was kept safe there.
Only foreign missionaries were involved; Rwandan believers themselves had no part in it, either way.
chat.meaning: In some churches people were massacred; some clergy took part, while other believers hid people and some died for it. Churches now run reconciliation work.
